deep.reconstruction:
This is a clean rewrite of the start of the previous page, preparing the Hilbert tensor product of two (pre)Hilbert spaces.

(1) For complex vector spaces E and F, write \bar E for the complex-conjugate space: the same additive group, with scalar multiplication λ·\bar x = \overline{\bar λ x}. Then \overline{E⊗F} ≅ \bar E⊗\bar F canonically. The map (\bar x,\bar y) ↦ \overline{x⊗y} is bilinear on \bar E×\bar F, so it induces a linear map \bar E⊗\bar F → \overline{E⊗F}. The previous page completes the argument: checking on bases shows this map is an isomorphism.

(2) If E carries a positive hermitian (sesquilinear) form (x,y), put (\bar x,\bar y) := (y,x) = \overline{(x,y)}. This is again sesquilinear and positive on \bar E, since (\bar x,\bar x) = (x,x). So \bar E is pre-Hilbert, and ‖\bar x‖ = ‖x‖. Hence \bar E is separated or complete exactly when E is, and \bar E is Hilbert when E is.

(3) For E Hilbert, the Riesz map y ↦ (·,y) is an antilinear isometry of E onto the dual E'. Equivalently, it is a linear isometric isomorphism \bar E ≅ E', which carries the Hilbert structure to E'.

Purpose: to put a canonical pre-Hilbert structure on E⊗F, one needs a linear form on (E⊗F)⊗\overline{E⊗F} ≅ (E⊗\bar E)⊗(F⊗\bar F). Elements of E⊗F are then read as maps \bar E' = E → F. The pencil note on the previous page ('E⊗F ⊂ L(\bar E',F)', 'Tr(u*u)') points to this Hilbert–Schmidt interpretation of the completed Hilbert tensor product.
errors: No mathematical errors. The definition (\bar x,\bar y) = (y,x) is the correct one that keeps the form linear in the first variable. Writing \overline{(y,x)} = (x,y) instead would give the wrong variance. The image shows (y,x).
